item.title: Mexico’s President Unveils Plan to Fight Seaweed That Is Choking Beaches
item.description: The seaweed — a stinky, brown algae known as sargassum — has plagued Mexico and the broader region for more than a decade, but this year’s forecast is setting records.
item.dc:creator: David Shortell
item.media:description: Sargassum seaweed covering the shoreline of a beach in Puerto Morelos, Mexico, this month.

item.title: Former Officials Protest U.S. Plan to Defund Pan American Health Organization
item.description: The group of former health and national security officials warned that Americans will be more vulnerable to infectious disease threats.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva Mandavilli
item.media:description: The Pan American Health Organization headquarters in Washington. The United States owes nearly $135 million in overdue fees to the organization.

item.title: Mistaken Username Sent Man to Prison for 18 Months, Court Finds
item.description: An appeals court in Canada acquitted Brandon Klayme of charges related to child sexual abuse imagery. His Kik username had one less underscore than another account that was involved.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor
item.media:credit: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press, via ZUMA Press
item.media:description: The Nova Scotia provincial flag. Prosecutors in Nova Scotia acknowledged the conviction had been flawed.

item.title: Cuba to Trump: We’re Open for Business
item.description: A top Cuban official says the island won’t negotiate its politics, but it is willing to talk investment, including from President Trump.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas
item.media:credit: Lisette Poole González for The New York Times
item.media:description: Carlos Fernández de Cossío, Cuba’s deputy foreign minister, in the Fidel Castro museum in Havana.

item.title: Cuba’s Bet on Solar
item.description: President Trump keeps predicting Cuba will collapse after he cut off its oil. But it’s still standing. Our reporter Jack Nicas visited to see how Cubans are adopting solar to offset the power shortage.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Alex Pena, Estelle Caswell, Thomas Vollkommer, James Surdam and Lisette Poole González

item.title: Canada’s Answer to Trump’s Tariffs: More Energy Deals With Europe
item.description: The Carney government’s agreement with a German natural gas company will also reduce Europe’s dependence on a Qatari supply made more uncertain by war.
item.dc:creator: Ian Austen
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:description: L.N.G. Canada’s export facility on Canada’s Pacific Coast in Kitimat, British Columbia.

item.title: St. Mary’s, Newfoundland, Will No Longer Reek of Rotten Fish Sauce
item.description: In Newfoundland, 20-year-old smelly sludge will finally be removed.
item.dc:creator: Victor Mather
item.media:credit: Elling Lien/The Canadian Press, via Associated Press
item.media:description: The process of draining and removing decades-old fish sauce has begun in Newfoundland.

item.title: As Trump Squeezes Cuba, He Plans to Send Cuban Deportees to Uruguay
item.description: The State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio has deported Cubans to Africa. Now it’s negotiating with a South American country.
item.dc:creator: Edward Wong and Emma Bubola
item.media:credit: Eric Lee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States had many concerns about Cuba, which is 90 miles from Florida, including “the threat of mass migration.”

item.title: The Cuban Throwing Parties to Fight for Political Change
item.description: David González has suddenly become the host of Havana’s hottest parties amid its energy crisis. Can he turn them into a movement?
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas
item.media:credit: Lisette Poole González for The New York Times
item.media:description: David González, 29, runs El Proyecto in Havana.

item.title: A Movie Night in Cuba’s Blackout
item.description: Amid the energy crisis caused by the Trump administration’s oil blockade of Cuba, our correspondent Jack Nicas visits a children’s movie night in a Havana neighborhood made possible by one family’s modified generator.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Alex Pena and Coleman Lowndes

item.title: How to Tell if a Giant Manta Is Pregnant? Give Her an Ultrasound.
item.description: Scientists managed to confirm pregnancies in three giant mantas with underwater ultrasound scans, offering clues to the animals’ elusive reproductive habits.
item.dc:creator: Alexa Robles-Gil

item.title: In This Costa Rican Forest, Monkeys Come Face-to-Face With A.I.
item.description: CapuchinAI, a portable testing station equipped with a touch screen and facial recognition software, could help scientists study primate intelligence in the wild.
item.dc:creator: Emily Anthes

item.title: Aquariums Are Relocating 30 Beluga Whales in ‘Unprecedented’ Rescue
item.description: Relocating the whales from a closed marine attraction in Canada to aquariums in the United States and Spain requires coordination, permits and a police escort.
item.dc:creator: Remy Tumin

item.title: Cubans Aren’t Sleeping in Sweltering Blackouts
item.description: Our reporter Jack Nicas visits a sweltering Cuba where, six months into the Trump administration’s oil blockade, people struggle to sleep with no electricity for fans or air-conditioning.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Leila Medina and Alex Pena

item.title: Shots Fired Outside U.S. Consulate in Canada for Second Time This Year
item.description: The police said that it was too early to say if the episode was linked to a shooting that targeted the diplomatic post in March.
item.dc:creator: Ian Austen
item.media:description: A cordoned-off area on University Avenue near the scene of the shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on Monday. The police said the attack had caused “some damage” to the facade of the building.

item.title: Guyana Ferry Tragedy Exposes Political Rifts in Oil-Rich Country
item.description: The capsizing of a ferry was Guyana’s deadliest event since Jonestown in 1978. Many are asking how this could happen in one of the world’s fastest-growing economies.
item.dc:creator: Simon Romero and César Rodríguez
item.media:credit: Cesar Rodriguez for The New York Times
item.media:description: A vigil for people who died in ferry sinking this month in Georgetown, Guyana.

item.title: Cuba, Lacking Fuel, Relies on Ingenuity to Defy Trump’s Blockade
item.description: President Trump has tried to strangle Cuba by blocking its oil imports. But six months later, the island is finding ways to endure.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Alex Pena and Lisette Poole González
item.media:credit: Lisette Poole González for The New York Times
item.media:description: An empty gas station in Havana.

item.title: How Cubans Are Surviving a Fuel Crisis
item.description: Cubans are inventing ways to survive without fuel or electricity, using solar panels, makeshift generators and batteries to endure a devastating oil blockade imposed by the Trump administration.
item.dc:creator: Jack Nicas, Alex Pena and Yasu Tsuji

item.title: Brazil Blocks Visit by U.S. Delegation Seeking to Question Election System
item.description: Brazilian authorities refused to grant visas to two senior U.S. officials out of concern they planned to sow doubt about the security of the country’s voting systems.
item.dc:creator: Ana Ionova, Adam B. Ellick and Jack Nicas
item.media:credit: Dado Galdieri for The New York Times
item.media:description: Police officers in the Brazilian capital, Brasília, last year. Ahead of presidential elections this year, Brazilian officials are concerned about possible attempts by U.S. officials to undermine confidence in the voting system.

item.title: As Trump Escalates Trade War With Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford Wants to Retaliate
item.description: While Mark Carney weighs his next steps, some provincial leaders point to oil, electricity and potash as powerful leverage against U.S. economic pressure.
item.dc:creator: Ian Austen
item.media:description: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and President Trump in the Oval Office at the White House on Oct. 7, 2025.

item.title: Colombia’s Trump-Endorsed President-Elect Was Once Investigated by U.S. Authorities
item.description: Colombia’s president-elect, a lawyer, represented accused drug traffickers, among others. While living in Miami, he himself was investigated by U.S. authorities, though never charged.
item.dc:creator: Annie Correal and David Ovalle
item.media:description: The Colombian president-elect Abelardo De La Espriella with a sign for his political movement, Defenders of the Homeland.

item.title: Argentines Facing Surge of Criticism After World Cup Loss Have Something to Say
item.description: Many Argentines condemned their players’ racist chants and aggressive behavior during the World Cup, but rejected what felt like a sweeping stigmatization of their entire nation.
item.dc:creator: Emma Bubola and Daniel Politi
item.media:credit: Sebastián López Brach for The New York Times
item.media:description: Argentine supporters at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Argentina, after the World Cup final on Sunday.

item.title: With Hopes High for New H.I.V. Prevention Pill, Merck Takes Steps to Ensure Access
item.description: Companies in Africa and India will make generic versions of the pill that could cost as little as $5 per person per year. But access to the drug and other new products in much of Latin America remains uncertain.

item.media:credit: Arlette Bashizi for The New York Times
item.media:description: Health workers speaking with students about H.I.V. prevention drugs at the University of Zambia in Lusaka in March.

item.title: As Canada Opens Gordie Howe International Bridge, Americans Are Told to Stay Home

item.dc:creator: Ian Austen

item.title: Venezuela’s Earthquakes Show Wealth Divide, Even in Death

item.media:credit: Adriana Loureiro Fernandez for The New York Times
item.media:description: Michell Mendoza, 16, right, standing next to a truck holding her mother’s coffin after being turned away from a cemetery.
